episode_title: Fault When a Pedestrian Is Hit

segment_1.topic_phrase: how the blame actually gets divided when somebody on foot is hit
segment_1.setup: I'm **{{INTERVIEWER}}**, and today's subject catches people completely off guard. In Florida, being hit while you were on foot doesn't automatically mean the driver was at fault, and how much of the blame lands on you changes everything.
segment_1.credential: **{{ATTORNEY}}**, your firm has accident reconstruction experts lined up before most clients even realize fault is being disputed.
segment_1.prompt: Somebody is in a hospital bed and the insurer has already decided how much of this was their fault. Tell us how they come up with that percentage. And if you've torn one of those numbers apart, take us through it.

attributes.name: Tried a contested split
attributes.detail: Cases you took to a jury, and what they did with a fault split the insurer thought was settled.

attributes.name: Blamed-pedestrian cases
attributes.detail: Not injury cases generally. Cases where the insurer put it on the person walking, how many, and how recently.

attributes.name: Verifiable record
attributes.detail: Your license and disciplinary history, verifiable in a way a testimonial never is.

attributes.name: What a jury here forgives
attributes.detail: The county court, the judges, and how a local jury reacts to somebody who was partly in the wrong.

attributes.name: Rebuilding the percentage
attributes.detail: How you take an insurer's number apart and put a defensible one in its place.

attributes.name: Sightlines and reconstruction
attributes.detail: Crash reconstruction experts, the people who figure out what a driver could actually see, and the treating doctors.

attributes.name: Witnesses fade
attributes.detail: What you secure in the first days, because memory of where somebody stood is gone inside a week.

attributes.name: Coverage with no car
attributes.detail: How a person with no vehicle of their own still reaches coverage, and whose policy it comes out of.

attributes.name: Both clocks
attributes.detail: The two-week medical window and the filing deadline, and the separate, much shorter deadline when a city, county or state agency is involved.

attributes.name: Fees and case costs
attributes.detail: What the percentage is, whether that percentage goes up if you file suit, who pays for the reconstruction, and what happens if you lose.

attributes.name: Who argues with the adjuster
attributes.detail: Whether the client is hiring you or an intake operation, and who actually fights the percentage.

attributes.name: When the client's share is high
attributes.detail: If a big share of the blame is genuinely going to land on the client, tell them the honest number instead of making a promise.

questions.q: How does anyone decide who was at fault when somebody is hit in Stuart?

bullets.label: Start with where they were
bullets.detail: the point of impact relative to the crossing does more work than any statement.

bullets.label: Then what each side could see
bullets.detail: sightlines, parked cars, lighting and the angle the driver was coming from.

bullets.label: Then who's investigating
bullets.detail: Stuart Police, the Martin County Sheriff's Office or the Highway Patrol, depending on the road, and if somebody was killed it goes to the Highway Patrol's traffic homicide investigators.

questions.q: Is the driver always at fault when somebody on foot gets hit?

bullets.label: No, and that surprises people
bullets.detail: being hit'sn't the same as being in the right, and the insurer knows it.

bullets.label: Fault comes down to a choice
bullets.detail: maybe the driver was speeding, looking at a phone, or turning without checking, or maybe the person on foot crossed where the driver couldn't see them.

bullets.label: Usually it's split
bullets.detail: most of these cases end up with some blame on each side, and the whole fight is over how big each side's share is.

questions.q: Can somebody on foot be found partly at fault for their own injuries in Florida?

bullets.label: Yes, and it's the usual outcome
bullets.detail: a share gets assigned to each side and yours comes straight off what you recover.

bullets.label: There's a hard cutoff
bullets.detail: past a certain share of the blame in Florida you recover nothing at all.

bullets.label: That's why the fight is over a few points
bullets.detail: insurers push you toward that line on purpose, and around here their favorite argument is that you crossed away from a marked crosswalk on a road where the crosswalks are a long way apart.

questions.q: What happens to your claim if you crossed against the signal?

bullets.label: It hurts your case, it doesn't end it
bullets.detail: your share of the blame goes up, and what you recover comes down by the same amount.

bullets.label: The driver still had duties
bullets.detail: a green light in their favor doesn't give them the right to hit somebody they could see.

bullets.label: The margin is what counts
bullets.detail: the argument is over ten or fifteen points, and that's real money either way.

questions.q: What happens when somebody crossed mid-block in Stuart?

bullets.label: You gave up the right of way
bullets.detail: away from a crosswalk the person on foot is the one required to yield, so some of the blame does get assigned to them.

bullets.label: The driver isn't excused
bullets.detail: they still had to be looking, and a driver who never braked has a problem of their own.

bullets.label: Why people do it here
bullets.detail: on US 1 the shops sit between the signals, so people cross where they need to be rather than walking a quarter mile to a light.

questions.q: What does the police report actually decide about fault?

bullets.label: Less than everybody assumes
bullets.detail: the officer got there afterward and wrote down what they were told.

bullets.label: It rarely reaches a jury
bullets.detail: the report itself usually never gets shown to the jury, so we rebuild the case from the evidence the officer was working from.

bullets.label: It still sets the opening number
bullets.detail: the adjuster reads it before anyone files anything, and if the injured person is from out of town, they will lean on that report hard.

questions.q: How do witnesses and video settle a disputed fault case in Stuart?

bullets.label: Video ends the argument
bullets.detail: the storefronts, restaurants and banks along US 1 and Kanner Highway hold most of it, and it's gone in about a month.

bullets.label: Witnesses fade fast
bullets.detail: memory of where somebody was standing degrades within days, and people move away.

bullets.label: Get both immediately
bullets.detail: send a written preservation letter on day one, because that's the difference between video that exists somewhere and video you actually get to use.

questions.q: How does a distracted driver shift the blame in Stuart and across the Treasure Coast?

bullets.label: It removes their best defense
bullets.detail: a driver who never looked up can't argue you appeared out of nowhere.

bullets.label: We can check the phone
bullets.detail: the carrier records show exactly what that phone was doing in the seconds before impact, and we can subpoena them.

bullets.label: Where it clusters here
bullets.detail: US 1 and Kanner Highway, where drivers are moving fast past shops and restaurants that people walk back and forth between.

questions.q: How much does the driver's speed change the fault picture?

bullets.label: It decides whether stopping was possible
bullets.detail: a few miles an hour is the difference between a driver stopping in time and never having a chance.

bullets.label: Speed is measurable
bullets.detail: the car's own computer stores it, the skid marks show it, and a reconstruction puts an actual number on it.

bullets.label: It also changes the injuries
bullets.detail: the same kind of collision at a higher speed produces a very different set of injuries, and that's something we can prove.

questions.q: How is fault worked out in a parking lot or a driveway?

bullets.label: The traffic laws don't apply the same way
bullets.detail: a private lot has no marked lanes and no signals, so there's a lot more room to argue.

bullets.label: Reversing is the common one
bullets.detail: a driver backing out has almost no view of what's directly behind them.

bullets.label: Cameras carry these
bullets.detail: the shopping center and restaurant lots along US 1 keep cameras, and that footage is the whole case when there's no independent witness.
